title: Special investigations: vitality tests, photos & models
blurb: Thermal and electric pulp tests, percussion, radiographs, study models, photographs, biopsies and blood tests: how each works, your role, and recording results.
question: A patient has toothache in the lower left. The dentist asks you to prepare for cold and electric pulp tests on 36 and a periapical radiograph. The patient mentions she has a pacemaker. What do you prepare, which tooth is tested first, and what do you do about the pacemaker?

teach.h: Tests that help the dentist decide
teach.body: Special investigations are tests beyond looking and charting that help the dentist reach a diagnosis and plan treatment. They include vitality (sensibility) tests, percussion, radiographs, study models, photographs, biopsies, swabs and blood tests. Your job is to prepare the right equipment, explain what will happen, support the patient, and record the results accurately. Interpreting the results and making the diagnosis is the dentist's role.

teach.h: Vitality tests test nerves, not blood supply
teach.body: A tooth is vital because of its blood supply, but cold, heat and electric tests only show whether the pulp nerves respond. So results can mislead. A false negative (no response from a living tooth) is common after recent trauma, in young teeth with open apices, and in heavily restored or crowned teeth. A false positive (a response from a dead tooth) can come from an anxious patient, a probe touching the gum or a metal filling, or saliva. That's why a control tooth is always tested first.

teach.h: Reading a cold test (the dentist interprets)
teach.caption: Record exactly what the patient reported, for each tooth tested, including the control.
A non-vital tooth with a periapical abscess: no response to cold or the electric pulp test, often tender to percussion, and a dark area at the root tip on a periapical radiograph.
Periapical views show the whole tooth, including the root apices and the surrounding bone, so they are used to look for infection at the root tip.

teach.body: Study models are made by casting alginate impressions in dental plaster or stone, then trimming and labelling them. They give a permanent 3D record of the teeth and bite for treatment planning, orthodontic assessment, monitoring tooth wear, making appliances and explaining treatment to patients. Clinical photographs record conditions before and after treatment. They need the patient's consent, cheek retractors and mirrors (warmed to stop misting), and must be stored securely as part of the clinical record.

A biopsy removes tissue for laboratory examination: incisional takes part of a lesion, excisional removes it all. The specimen goes into a labelled pot of formalin (formal saline, a COSHH-controlled hazardous chemical) with a completed pathology request form. Blood tests are usually arranged through the GP or hospital, for example a full blood count, a glucose test for suspected diabetes, or an INR check for a patient on warfarin before extractions. Swabs check for infection such as candida.

teach.text: No response to a vitality test does not automatically mean the tooth is dead, and a response doesn't prove it is healthy. Always test a control tooth first, keep the tooth dry, and record what you observe. The dentist puts the results together with the history and radiographs.

items: Vitality tests: cold, heat, electric. They test nerve response, not blood supply.
Test a control tooth first; isolate and dry; record each tooth's result.
Pacemaker? Tell the dentist before any electric pulp test.
Percussion tenderness suggests inflammation round the root.
Study models and photos are records: consent, label, store securely.
Biopsy specimens go in labelled formalin with a request form.

summary: You can now prepare for and support vitality tests, explain why control teeth and dry fields matter, recognise false results, and handle study models, photographs, biopsy specimens and requests for blood tests safely and accurately.

A.q: Before electric pulp testing 36, which tooth should usually be tested first?
options: The tooth next to 36 on the same side
A healthy control tooth, such as 46
The most heavily restored tooth
Any tooth with a crown
A.why: A healthy control tooth, often the same tooth on the other side, shows the patient what a normal response feels like and gives a baseline to compare.

whyNot.0: A neighbouring tooth may share the problem, so it isn't a reliable control.
whyNot.2: Heavily restored teeth often give false negative results.
whyNot.3: Full crowns usually stop the electric pulp test giving a reliable reading.

A.q: What do cold and electric pulp tests actually assess?
options: The blood flow inside the pulp
The density of the surrounding bone
The depth of the periodontal pocket
The response of the pulp nerves
A.why: These sensibility tests show whether the pulp nerves respond; they don't measure blood supply directly.

whyNot.0: Blood flow isn't measured by cold or EPT, which is why false results happen.
whyNot.2: Pocket depth is measured with a periodontal probe.

A.q: A patient's tooth is very tender when the dentist taps it with the end of a mirror handle. What does this suggest?
options: A healthy, vital pulp
Enamel caries only
Inflammation round the root
Dentine hypersensitivity
A.why: Tenderness to percussion suggests inflammation of the tissues round the root apex or periodontal ligament.

whyNot.0: A healthy tooth isn't tender to percussion.
whyNot.1: Enamel caries doesn't cause tenderness to tapping.
whyNot.3: Hypersensitivity causes sharp pain to cold or touch on exposed dentine, not tenderness to tapping.

B.q: Why is the tooth dried and isolated before an electric pulp test?
options: Saliva can conduct current to the gum
A dry tooth feels the current less
It stops the probe slipping off
It makes the reading last longer
B.why: Moisture can carry the current to the gum or neighbouring teeth, giving a false positive reading.

whyNot.1: Drying is about accuracy, not reducing the sensation.
whyNot.2: The conducting medium, not dryness, keeps good contact.
whyNot.3: Drying doesn't affect how long the reading lasts.

B.q: A tooth that was knocked a week ago gives no response to cold or EPT. Why might this be misleading?
options: Trauma always leaves a tooth non-vital
Cold tests are unreliable on front teeth
Electric tests only work on back teeth
Injured teeth can give false negatives
B.why: After trauma the nerves may temporarily stop responding even though the pulp may recover, so the tooth is reviewed and retested.

whyNot.0: Many traumatised teeth stay vital; that's why they are monitored.
whyNot.1: Cold tests are routinely and reliably used on front teeth.
whyNot.2: Electric pulp tests can be used on front and back teeth.

B.q: An incisional biopsy has been taken. How should the specimen be sent?
options: In a dry, labelled envelope
In sterile saline in the fridge
In labelled formalin with a request form
Wrapped in damp gauze in the outgoing post tray
B.why: Biopsy specimens are fixed in a labelled pot of formalin and sent with a completed pathology request form.

whyNot.0: A dry specimen deteriorates and can't be examined properly.
whyNot.1: Saline doesn't preserve tissue for histopathology.
whyNot.3: Gauze gives no preservation and is a safety and confidentiality risk.

C.q: A patient booked for an electric pulp test tells you she has a pacemaker. What should you do?
options: Carry on as the current is tiny
Ask her to hold the probe herself
Use the cold test only, without telling anyone
Tell the dentist before the test
C.why: A pacemaker is relevant medical history, so the dentist must know and decide whether the electric test is appropriate.

whyNot.0: You can't make that judgement; the dentist must be told.
whyNot.1: Changing who holds the probe doesn't address the medical concern.
whyNot.2: Choosing the test is the dentist's decision and must be recorded.

C.q: What is the main purpose of study models?
options: To replace the need for radiographs in future
To test the vitality of the teeth
To give a 3D record of the teeth and bite
To show the bone round the roots
C.why: Study models give a lasting three-dimensional record of the teeth and occlusion for planning and monitoring.

whyNot.0: Models show the crowns of the teeth, not what radiographs show.
whyNot.1: Vitality is tested with cold, heat or EPT.
whyNot.3: Bone round the roots is seen on radiographs.

C.q: Which investigation is the dentist most likely to arrange through the GP for a patient on warfarin before extractions?
options: An INR blood test
A cold vitality test
A bitewing radiograph
A saliva flow test
C.why: The INR shows how long the blood takes to clot in a patient on warfarin, which affects bleeding risk after extractions.

whyNot.1: Vitality tests assess the pulp, not bleeding risk.
whyNot.2: Bitewings show caries and bone levels, not clotting.
whyNot.3: Saliva tests relate to caries risk, not bleeding.

reteach.title: A vitality test is like knocking on a door
reteach.question: If you knock on a door and nobody answers, does that prove nobody lives there? How does that help you understand pulp tests?

blocks.body: Cold and EPT knock on the pulp's door and listen for the nerves to answer. A healthy pulp answers quickly and then goes quiet. An inflamed pulp answers loudly and keeps complaining (lingering pain). No answer may mean nobody's home (a dead pulp), but the person inside might just be stunned after an injury, or the door might be too thick, like a big filling or a crown. So you always knock on a neighbour's door first (the control tooth) to know what a normal answer sounds like.

blocks.text: Electric pulp test numbers aren't a 'health score'. They're compared with the control tooth and judged by the dentist alongside symptoms and radiographs.

explain.body: Cold (ethyl chloride or a refrigerant spray on a cotton pledget) and heat (warmed gutta-percha) test the pulp's nerve response. A short, sharp response that fades is normal; pain that lingers suggests an inflamed pulp.

explain.caption: Deep caries reaching the pulp often causes lingering pain to hot and cold.

test.q: What is commonly used to carry out a cold test?
options: Ethyl chloride on a cotton pledget
Warmed gutta-percha on the tooth
A periodontal probe in the pocket
Air from the 3-in-1 syringe only
test.why: Ethyl chloride or a refrigerant spray on a cotton pledget gives a strong cold stimulus to a single tooth.

whyNot.1: Warmed gutta-percha is used for the heat test.
whyNot.3: Air alone is not a reliable controlled cold test.

explain.body: Check medical history, test a control tooth, isolate and dry, put conducting medium on the probe, place it on enamel, let the patient complete the circuit, raise the current slowly, record the reading.

test.q: Where on the tooth is the electric pulp tester probe placed?
options: On a metal filling if present
On the gum next to the tooth
On sound enamel of the crown
Inside the root canal
test.why: The probe goes on sound enamel, usually on the buccal or labial surface, with a conducting medium.

whyNot.0: Metal conducts current to neighbouring teeth or gum, giving false results.
whyNot.1: Touching the gum gives a false positive.
whyNot.3: EPT is a non-invasive surface test.

explain.body: Study models record the teeth and bite in 3D. Photographs record before and after. Both need consent, labelling and secure storage as part of the patient's record.

test.q: What must be obtained before taking clinical photographs of a patient?
options: A radiograph of the area
The patient's consent
A signed lab prescription
A referral from the GP
test.why: Clinical photographs are personal data and part of the record, so the patient's consent is needed.

whyNot.0: A radiograph is a separate investigation, not a requirement for photos.
whyNot.2: Lab prescriptions are for laboratory work.
whyNot.3: No GP referral is needed for clinical photographs.

explain.body: Biopsy: incisional (part) or excisional (whole). Specimen in labelled formalin with a request form. Blood tests such as FBC, glucose or INR are usually arranged via the GP or hospital.

options: A photograph of the lesion
Removal of part of the lesion
A swab of the lesion surface
Removal of the whole lesion
test.why: An excisional biopsy removes the entire lesion for examination.

whyNot.0: A photograph is a record, not a biopsy.
whyNot.1: Removing part of a lesion is an incisional biopsy.
whyNot.2: A swab collects surface cells or microbes, not tissue.
